title: Measurement-Consistent Langevin Corrector for Stabilizing Latent Diffusion Inverse Problem Solvers
claim: Without correction, the sampler's intermediate trajectory is noisy and artifact-ridden; adding our corrector yields clean, structured intermediates that converge to a coherent output.
layout: 2 rows by 10 columns, left-to-right over timesteps, row labels Base/Ours
description: A wide strip of image grids with two rows and ten columns. Column headers give diffusion timesteps t=1000, 980, 960, down to 820. The left labels read 'Base' for the top row and 'Ours' for the bottom row. Each cell shows a single latent channel in a viridis-like blue, purple and yellow colormap. At t=1000 both rows show the same noisy latent. In the Base row, later frames stay speckled, with grid-like patterns and blocky noise. They show only a faint, fragmented face. In the Ours row, the frames become smoother and more structured. A clear face with hair and shoulders emerges by t≈880 and sharpens through t=820. The eye goes to the contrast between the noisy top row and the clean face in the bottom row.
caption: Reverse dynamics of LDM-based inverse problem solver, PSLD. We visualize the reverse sampling trajectory of z0|t for the latent diffusion inverse solver, PSLD (Rout et al., 2023). The naive dynamics of the solver exhibit undesirable artifacts (first row), whereas the solver corrected with MCLC yields cleaner and more structured latents (second row). For clarity, only the fourth channel is visualized.
abstract: While latent diffusion models (LDMs) have emerged as powerful priors for inverse problems, existing LDM-based solvers frequently suffer from instability. In this work, we first identify the instability as a discrepancy between the solver dynamics and stable reverse diffusion dynamics learned by the diffusion model, and show that reducing this gap stabilizes the solver. Building on this, we introduce \textit{Measurement-Consistent Langevin Corrector (MCLC)}, a theoretically grounded plug-and-play stabilization module that remedies the LDM-based inverse problem solvers through measurement-consistent Langevin updates. Compared to prior approaches that rely on linear manifold assumptions, which often fail to hold in latent space, MCLC provides a principled stabilization mechanism, leading to more stable and reliable behavior in latent space.
